steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a fairness-in-ML paper arguing that variance, i.e. arbitrariness in predictions, confounds how we evaluate fair binary classification. Open with a motivating example, pose our research question, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Fair binary classification: fairness metrics vs. model confidence
- Motivating example: many models on COMPAS, two individuals
- Single-model evaluation hides arbitrariness; research question
- Contributions 1-2: self-consistency metric, ensembling with abstention
- Contributions 3-4: large experimental study, HMDA dataset package

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Algorithmic fairness
  - goal: techniques to measure and mitigate discrimination in automated decision-making
  - fair binary classification: train model to satisfy chosen fairness metric; parity of error rates across demographic groups (cite)
  - satisfying a metric != equally confident in each classification

- Example (Figure 1)
  - 100 logistic regression models, same learning process, different subsamples of training set, COMPAS prison recidivism dataset (cite)
  - compare classifications for two test individuals
  - Individual 1: all agree "will recidivate"; Individual 2: complete disagreement
  - pick one model at random: no effect on Individual 1, effectively random for Individual 2
  - learning process not confident enough to justify either outcome for Individual 2
  - such instances: classification effectively arbitrary (cite)
  - arbitrariness -> discrimination if systematically more arbitrary for some demographic groups

- Single model
  - example uses one model; typical setup; popular metrics evaluate fairness of a single model (cite)
  - single model masks arbitrariness
  - need distributions over possible models for a learning process
  - question: What is the empirical role of arbitrariness in fair binary classification tasks?

- Contributions 1-2
  - 1. Quantify arbitrariness: self-consistency, from statistical variance, proxy for arbitrariness; simple yet powerful (Section 3)
  - 2. Ensemble to improve self-consistency: extend classic bagging (cite) with abstention when self-consistency low; better self-consistency (less variance) and accuracy (Section 4)

- Contributions 3-4
  - 3. Comprehensive experimental study of variance in fair binary classification; largest to date; self-consistency and arbitrariness
    - most benchmarks close-to-fair once arbitrariness accounted for, before any fairness interventions (Section 5)
    - casts doubt on prior work claiming baseline unfairness to show fairness methods work
    - such methods often empirically unnecessary (Section 6)
  - 4. Release large-scale fairness dataset package: variance (esp. small datasets) undermines reliability; open-source package for US Home Mortgage Disclosure Act datasets (HMDA)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
One goal of algorithmic fairness is developing techniques to measure and mitigate discrimination in automated decision-making. In fair binary classification, this often means training a model so that it satisfies a chosen fairness metric, and these metrics typically define fairness as parity between the model's error rates for different demographic groups in the dataset. But even if the classifications of a model satisfy some fairness metric, that does not necessarily mean the model is equally confident in each classification.

To give an intuition for what we mean by confidence, consider this experiment. We fit 100 logistic regression models with the same learning process, which draws different subsamples of the training set from the COMPAS prison recidivism dataset, and we then compare the classifications we get for two individuals in the test set. Figure 1 shows that the consistency of predictions is different for the two individuals: the 100 models agree completely to classify Individual 1 as “will recidivate”, and they disagree completely on whether Individual 2 should be classified as “will” or “will not recidivate.” If we picked one model at random to use in practice, how Individual 1 is classified would not be affected; but for Individual 2 the prediction is effectively random. We can interpret this disagreement as meaning that the learning process that produced the predictions is not confident enough to justify assigning either decision outcome to Individual 2. In practice instances like Individual 2 show so little confidence that their classification is effectively arbitrary. Also, this arbitrariness can bring about discrimination too, if the classification decisions are systematically more arbitrary for individuals in certain demographic groups.

  - single model masks arbitrariness
  - need distributions over possible models for a learning process
  - question: What is the empirical role of arbitrariness in fair binary classification tasks?

  - 2. Ensemble to improve self-consistency: extend classic bagging (cite) with abstention when self-consistency low; better self-consistency (less variance) and accuracy (Section 4)

- Contributions 3-4

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
One goal of algorithmic fairness is developing techniques to measure and mitigate discrimination in automated decision-making. In fair binary classification, this often means training a model so that it satisfies a chosen fairness metric, and these metrics typically define fairness as parity between the model's error rates for different demographic groups in the dataset. But even if the classifications of a model satisfy some fairness metric, that does not necessarily mean the model is equally confident in each classification.

To give an intuition for what we mean by confidence, consider this experiment. We fit 100 logistic regression models with the same learning process, which draws different subsamples of the training set from the COMPAS prison recidivism dataset, and we then compare the classifications we get for two individuals in the test set. Figure 1 shows that the consistency of predictions is different for the two individuals: the 100 models agree completely to classify Individual 1 as “will recidivate”, and they disagree completely on whether Individual 2 should be classified as “will” or “will not recidivate.” If we picked one model at random to use in practice, how Individual 1 is classified would not be affected; but for Individual 2 the prediction is effectively random. We can interpret this disagreement as meaning that the learning process that produced the predictions is not confident enough to justify assigning either decision outcome to Individual 2. In practice instances like Individual 2 show so little confidence that their classification is effectively arbitrary. Also, this arbitrariness can bring about discrimination too, if the classification decisions are systematically more arbitrary for individuals in certain demographic groups.

An important aspect of this example is that only one model is used to make predictions. This is the typical setup in fair binary classification: popular metrics are commonly applied to evaluate the fairness of a single model. However, as the example learning process in Figure 1 makes clear, using only one model can mask how arbitrary the predictions are. To reveal arbitrariness, we instead need to look at distributions over possible models for a given learning process. With this change in frame, we ask:

What is the empirical role of arbitrariness in fair binary classification tasks?

We make four contributions to study this question:

- 1. Quantify arbitrariness. We formalize a metric, self-consistency, which is derived from statistical variance, and we use it as a quantitative proxy for the arbitrariness of model outputs. Self-consistency is a simple tool but a powerful one for empirical analyses of fair classification (Section 3).

- 2. Ensemble to improve self-consistency. We extend the classic bagging method so that it can abstain from classifying instances where self-consistency is low. This improves self-consistency overall (i.e., it reduces variance), and it also improves accuracy (Section 4).

- 3. Perform a comprehensive experimental study of variance in fair binary classification. We do the largest such study to date, looking at it through self-consistency and its relationship to arbitrariness. Surprisingly, we find that most benchmarks are close to fair once we take into account how much arbitrariness is present in predictions — and this is before we even try applying any fairness interventions (Section 5). This finding is shocking and has huge implications for the field: it casts doubt on how reliable prior work is that claims there is baseline unfairness in these benchmarks in order to show that methods to improve fairness work in practice. What we find instead is that such methods are often empirically unnecessary for improving fairness (Section 6).

- 4. Release a large-scale fairness dataset package. We observe that variance, especially in small datasets, can undermine how reliable conclusions about fairness are. So we open-source a package that makes the large-scale US Home Mortgage Disclosure Act datasets (HMDA) easy to use for future research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A goal of algorithmic fairness is to develop techniques that measure and mitigate discrimination in automated decision-making. In fair binary classification, this often involves training a model to satisfy a chosen fairness metric, which typically defines fairness as parity between model error rates for different demographic groups in the dataset [1]. However, even if a model's classifications satisfy a particular fairness metric, the model is not necessarily equally confident in each classification.

To provide an intuition for what we mean by confidence, consider the following experiment: We fit 100 logistic regression models using the same learning process, which draws different subsamples of the training set from the COMPAS prison recidivism dataset [2,3], and we compare the resulting classifications for two individuals in the test set. Figure 1 shows a difference in the consistency of predictions for the two individuals: the 100 models agree completely to classify Individual 1 as “will recidivate” and disagree completely on whether to classify Individual 2 as “will” or “will not recidivate.” If we were to pick one model at random to use in practice, there would be no effect on how Individual 1 is classified; yet, for Individual 2, the prediction is effectively random. We can interpret this disagreement to mean that the learning process that produced these predictions is not confident enough to justify assigning Individual 2 either decision outcome. In practice, instances like Individual 2 exhibit so little confidence that their classification is effectively arbitrary [4,5,6]. Further, this arbitrariness can also bring about discrimination if classification decisions are systematically more arbitrary for individuals in certain demographic groups.

A key aspect of this example is that we use only one model to make predictions. This is the typical setup in fair binary classification: Popular metrics are commonly applied to evaluate the fairness of a single model [7,8,9]. However, as the example learning process in Figure 1 makes clear, using only a single model can mask the arbitrariness of predictions. To reveal arbitrariness, we must instead examine distributions over possible models for a given learning process. With this shift in frame, we ask:

What is the empirical role of arbitrariness in fair binary classification tasks?

To study this question, we make four contributions:

- 1. Quantify arbitrariness. We formalize a metric called self-consistency, derived from statistical variance, which we use as a quantitative proxy for the arbitrariness of model outputs. Self-consistency is a simple yet powerful tool for empirical analyses of fair classification (Section 3).

- 2. Ensemble to improve self-consistency. We extend [10]'s classic bagging so that it can abstain from classifying instances for which self-consistency is low. This improves overall self-consistency (i.e., reduces variance), and also improves accuracy (Section 4).

- 3. Perform a comprehensive experimental study of variance in fair binary classification. We conduct the largest such study to date, through the lens of self-consistency and its relationship to arbitrariness. Surprisingly, we find that most benchmarks are close-to-fair when the amount of arbitrariness present in predictions is taken into account — before we even try to apply any fairness interventions (Section 5). This shocking finding has huge implications for the field: it casts doubt on the reliability of prior work that claims there is baseline unfairness in these benchmarks in order to demonstrate that methods to improve fairness work in practice. We find instead that such methods are often empirically unnecessary to improve fairness (Section 6).

- 4. Release a large-scale fairness dataset package. We observe that variance, particularly in small datasets, can undermine the reliability of conclusions about fairness. We therefore open-source a package that makes the large-scale US Home Mortgage Disclosure Act datasets (HMDA) easy to use for future research.
